questions.q: What happens to a std::unique_ptr<Order>'s managed object when the pointer goes out of scope?
options: Nothing — you must call delete manually
It is automatically deleted, with no manual delete required
It is copied to a new unique_ptr automatically
It becomes a shared_ptr automatically
questions.explain: unique_ptr's defining feature is automatic cleanup: it deletes its managed object exactly once, when it goes out of scope, with no manual delete needed.

questions.q: What does std::move actually do to its argument?
options: It deep-copies the object to a new location
It immediately deletes the object
It casts the object to an rvalue reference, signaling that its contents may be transferred away
It makes the object const
questions.explain: std::move performs a cast to rvalue reference; it doesn't move anything by itself, but it enables move construction/assignment to transfer internals instead of deep-copying.

questions.q: In `for (const auto& [symbol, price] : prices)` over a `std::map<std::string, double>`, what C++17 feature is `[symbol, price]` an example of?
options: A lambda capture list
A structured binding, unpacking each pair's members into named variables
An initializer list
A template parameter pack
questions.explain: Structured bindings let you unpack a pair, tuple, or aggregate into individually named variables in a single declaration.

questions.q: Why is std::optional<double> generally preferable to using -1.0 as a sentinel for 'no price available'?
options: optional is faster to compute than a double comparison
-1.0 could be mistaken for a valid return value, while optional makes the absence of a value an explicit, checkable part of the type
optional uses less memory than a double
Sentinels are not allowed in C++17 or later
questions.explain: A sentinel value is just an ordinary value that could legitimately occur or be misread; std::optional encodes 'might have no value' directly in the type, forcing an explicit check.

questions.q: When should std::shared_ptr be preferred over std::unique_ptr?
options: Always, since shared_ptr is strictly more capable
Only when an object genuinely needs multiple simultaneous owners that share responsibility for its lifetime
Never — shared_ptr is deprecated in modern C++
Whenever the object is small
questions.explain: unique_ptr should be the default since it has zero overhead over a raw pointer; shared_ptr's reference counting overhead is only justified when genuine shared ownership is required.
